shortDef: Making a product usable by people with disabilities.
longDef: Accessibility covers vision, hearing, motor and cognitive differences, permanent and temporary alike. It is a baseline requirement rather than a feature, and in many jurisdictions a legal one. Built in from the start it costs little; retrofitted it is one of the most expensive things a team can do.
example: A form that can be completed with a keyboard, announced correctly by a screen reader, and read at 200% text size.
misuse: "a11y" is a numeronym — eleven letters between the a and the y — not an abbreviation to say aloud as a word.

shortDef: The international standard for accessible digital content.
longDef: WCAG organises testable success criteria under four principles and three conformance levels: A, AA and AAA. Most laws and procurement policies reference level AA, which is the practical target. Version 2.2 added criteria on focus appearance, dragging alternatives and minimum target size.
example: Meeting AA means 4.5:1 text contrast, visible focus, keyboard operability and no keyboard traps, among others.
misuse: Passing an automated checker is not conformance. Automated tools catch perhaps a third of the criteria.

shortDef: WCAG's four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, robust.
longDef: Content must be perceivable through more than one sense, operable by more than one input, understandable in language and behaviour, and robust enough to work with assistive technology now and later. Every WCAG criterion sits under one of the four. It is a useful diagnostic: when something fails, naming which principle broke usually points at the fix.
example: A video with no captions fails perceivable; a menu that only opens on hover fails operable.

shortDef: Software or hardware people use to operate a device.
longDef: Screen readers, magnifiers, switch devices, voice control, braille displays, eye-gaze systems and alternative keyboards all sit between the person and your interface. Each depends on the structure and names your product exposes, not on how it looks. Designing without knowing which technologies your audience uses is guessing.
example: A switch user navigates by scanning through focusable elements, so focus order and visible focus decide whether the app works.

shortDef: Software that speaks interface content aloud.
longDef: A screen reader builds a linear model of the interface from its structure — roles, names, states — and lets the user move through it by element, heading or landmark. What it announces comes from code, not appearance, so a visually obvious button with no accessible name is announced as "button". Testing with the real thing takes minutes and finds problems no checklist does.
example: Turning on VoiceOver and completing a search, reading a definition and saving it without looking at the screen.
misuse: Screen reader users do not read pages top to bottom. Most navigate by headings and landmarks, which is why structure matters.

shortDef: The text assistive technology announces for an element.
longDef: It comes from the visible label where there is one, and otherwise from an explicit attribute. Names must describe the outcome — "Save term", not "button" or "icon" — and should include the visible text so voice-control users can say what they see. Every interactive element needs one.
example: An icon-only close control given the name "Close settings" rather than being announced as an unlabelled button.
misuse: Adding a name that differs from the visible label breaks voice control, which matches on what is on screen.

shortDef: A text description of an image, for people who cannot see it.
longDef: Good alt text conveys the image's purpose in this context rather than describing every detail — the same photograph needs different alt text in a news story and a shop listing. Purely decorative images should be marked as such so they are skipped entirely. If the image carries information found nowhere else, that information belongs in the text.
example: A chart's alt text states the trend and the key figure, with the full data available in a table beneath it.
misuse: "Image of…" wastes the first two words — screen readers already announce that it is an image.

shortDef: Using elements for their meaning, not just their appearance.
longDef: A real button, heading or list carries role, state and keyboard behaviour for free, across every assistive technology and platform. Recreating them from generic containers means reimplementing all of that, usually incompletely. The first rule of ARIA is that not using ARIA is better — use the native element.
example: A button element responds to Enter and Space, is focusable, and is announced as a button, with no extra code.
misuse: A styled div with a click handler looks identical and is invisible to keyboard and screen-reader users.

shortDef: Attributes that describe roles, states and properties to assistive tech.
longDef: ARIA fills gaps where native elements cannot express a pattern — a tab set, a combobox, a live region. It changes what is announced, never what the element does, so keyboard behaviour still has to be built by hand. Misapplied ARIA is worse than none, because it overrides correct native semantics.
example: A custom tab list marked with the tablist, tab and tabpanel roles, plus arrow-key handling written to match.
misuse: Adding role="button" to a div does not make it focusable or operable by keyboard. It only changes the announcement.

shortDef: A labelled region letting users jump straight to part of a page.
longDef: Header, navigation, main, search and footer regions give screen-reader users a map and a way to skip whole sections in one gesture. They cost nothing when native elements are used. Multiple landmarks of the same type need distinct labels, or the map becomes ambiguous.
example: Jumping directly to main content, bypassing a navigation region, using a single rotor gesture.

shortDef: Headings nested in order, describing the shape of the content.
longDef: Headings are the primary way screen-reader users navigate, so levels must reflect meaning rather than the size that looked right. One top-level heading per screen, with no skipped levels, produces an outline that can be scanned in seconds. It benefits sighted users too, since the same structure drives visual hierarchy.
example: A term page with the headword as the page heading and Example, Related terms and Sources as second-level headings.
misuse: Choosing a heading level for its font size is the most common cause of broken outlines. Style and level are separate decisions.

shortDef: Operating everything without a mouse or touch.
longDef: Every interactive element must be reachable and usable by keyboard, in an order that matches the visual layout, with no trap that cannot be escaped. It is a requirement in itself and a proxy for switch access, voice control and screen readers, which all build on the same focus model. Unplugging the mouse for ten minutes is the cheapest audit available.
example: Tabbing through a form, opening a dropdown with arrow keys, and closing a dialog with Escape back to the trigger.
misuse: A custom control that is focusable but does nothing on Enter or Space is a keyboard failure, not a partial success.

shortDef: The visible marker showing which element the keyboard is on.
longDef: Without it, keyboard users cannot tell where they are. WCAG 2.2 requires the indicator to be clearly visible against both the element and its background, with enough contrast and area. Removing the default outline without providing a better one is a well-known and serious defect.
example: A two-pixel outline offset from the control, in a colour that meets 3:1 against both surfaces, in light and dark themes.
misuse: Suppressing focus outlines because they look untidy makes the product unusable for anyone not using a pointer.

shortDef: Moving keyboard focus deliberately when the interface changes.
longDef: When a dialog opens, focus moves into it and is contained there; when it closes, focus returns to what opened it. When content is replaced, focus goes to the new content rather than being dumped at the top. Getting this wrong silently strands keyboard and screen-reader users somewhere they cannot see.
example: Opening settings moves focus to its heading; closing it returns focus to the Settings button that was pressed.
misuse: A focus trap is correct inside a modal and a serious bug anywhere else, where it prevents leaving a component at all.

shortDef: A link that jumps past repeated navigation to the main content.
longDef: Usually the first focusable element and visually hidden until focused, it saves keyboard users from tabbing through the same navigation on every page. It must actually move focus, not just scroll. On apps with landmark regions it matters less, but it remains the cheapest fix for repetitive navigation.
example: Pressing Tab on load reveals "Skip to main content", which moves focus straight into the page body.

shortDef: An area whose updates are announced without moving focus.
longDef: Live regions let a screen reader report changes the user did not navigate to — a result count updating, a toast appearing, an error arriving. Polite announcements wait for a pause; assertive ones interrupt and should be rare. Too many live regions make a product unusable through constant chatter.
example: "12 results" announced politely as the user types, without pulling focus out of the search field.
misuse: A visual toast with no live region is silent for screen-reader users, which is the most common version of this bug.

shortDef: Reduced ability to distinguish certain colours.
longDef: Around one in twelve men and one in two hundred women have some form, most commonly difficulty separating red from green. The design consequence is simple and absolute: never let colour be the only thing carrying meaning. Add text, shape, position or pattern alongside it.
example: A status list that pairs each colour with a written label, so red and green are not the only difference.
misuse: Checking contrast ratios does not cover this. Two colours can pass contrast and still be indistinguishable to some viewers.

shortDef: Respecting the text size the user set at system level.
longDef: Many people run their phone at larger text permanently, and layouts must survive it — up to 200% is the usual requirement. That means no fixed heights on text containers, no truncation of essential content, and rows that stack when they run out of width. Testing at the largest setting exposes problems no other test does.
example: A list row that shows term and definition side by side at default size and stacks them at 200%.
misuse: Disabling font scaling to protect a layout is a defect, not a solution — it overrides a setting the user chose deliberately.

shortDef: Letting users increase line, word and letter spacing without breakage.
longDef: WCAG requires that content still work when line height is raised to 1.5 times the font size, paragraph spacing to twice, letter spacing to 0.12 and word spacing to 0.16. People with dyslexia and low vision use these settings routinely. Layouts built on fixed heights fail this immediately.
example: A card whose height grows with its content rather than clipping the third line when spacing increases.

shortDef: Honouring the system setting that suppresses animation.
longDef: Large parallax, zooming transitions and looping movement can trigger nausea, dizziness and migraine for people with vestibular disorders. When the setting is on, replace motion with an instant change or a simple fade rather than removing the feedback entirely. The setting exists on every major platform and is trivial to read.
example: A card flip becomes an immediate swap, and staggered list entrances render instantly, when reduced motion is on.
misuse: Reduced motion does not mean no feedback. Silently dropping the transition and its result leaves the user unsure what happened.

shortDef: Synchronised text of speech and meaningful sound in video.
longDef: Captions serve deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers, and in practice a large share of all viewers, who watch with sound off. Good captions include speaker changes and important non-speech sound, not just dialogue. Auto-generated captions need editing before they can be relied on, particularly for names and jargon.
example: "[door closes] Priya: I've sent the file" rather than dialogue alone.
misuse: Subtitles assume the viewer can hear and only translate speech; captions do not. The words are not interchangeable.

shortDef: A full text version of audio or video content.
longDef: A transcript can be read at the reader's pace, searched, translated and used with a braille display, which captions cannot. For video it should describe important visual information as well as speech. It is often the cheapest accessibility improvement for content-heavy products, and it helps search too.
example: A recorded research readout published with a transcript, so a finding can be found by searching for a phrase.

shortDef: Designing for differences in memory, attention and processing.
longDef: It covers people with learning disabilities, ADHD, autism, brain injury and age-related change — and everyone under stress or distraction. The practical measures are plain language, consistent patterns, generous time limits, undo instead of confirmation, and never requiring information to be held in memory across steps. It is the least automated and most impactful area of accessibility.
example: Showing the entered address on the confirmation step rather than asking the user to remember what they typed.

shortDef: Typographic and language choices that reduce reading effort.
longDef: The evidence supports generous line spacing, left-aligned unjustified text, short lines, clear everyday typefaces and reduced glare from pure white backgrounds. Support for specialist dyslexia typefaces is weak; ordinary well-set text tends to perform as well or better. Letting users adjust spacing and colour themselves is the most reliable measure.
example: Left-aligned body text at 1.55 line height on an off-white surface, with no justified columns.
misuse: Installing a "dyslexia font" is not a substitute for good typesetting, and research has not shown it to help.

shortDef: Operating a device with one or two physical buttons.
longDef: The system scans through focusable elements and the user selects with a switch, so every extra element in the focus order costs real time. It depends entirely on correct focus order, visible focus and reachable controls. Anything requiring a gesture, a drag or a hover is unavailable without an alternative.
example: Reducing a card from four focusable elements to one, with actions in a menu, halves the time to reach the next card.

shortDef: Operating an interface by speaking the names of controls.
longDef: Users say what they see — "tap Save term" — so the accessible name must contain the visible label. Controls with no visible text need a spoken alternative, and numbered overlays are the fallback when nothing matches. It is one of the strongest arguments for labelling icons.
example: "Tap Saved" works because the tab's accessible name starts with the word printed beneath it.
misuse: Giving an element an accessible name that differs from its visible label breaks voice control even though it reads fine.

shortDef: Designing for the full range of human diversity.
longDef: Where accessibility focuses on removing barriers for disabled people, inclusive design is the wider practice of building for varied abilities, contexts, languages and circumstances, and of involving those people in the work. Its central insight is that designing for a permanent constraint usually helps people with temporary and situational versions of it too. It is a method, not a compliance activity.
example: One-handed operation designed for a person with limited mobility also serves someone holding a child or a coffee.
misuse: Not a synonym for accessibility. Accessibility is a required outcome; inclusive design is one way of getting there.

shortDef: A structured assessment against a standard such as WCAG.
longDef: An audit combines automated scanning, manual keyboard and screen-reader testing, and judgement about criteria that cannot be automated. The output is a prioritised list of failures with the criterion each breaches. Testing with disabled users is a separate and complementary activity — an audit finds standard violations, not lived friction.
example: A report listing each failure, the WCAG criterion, the screens affected and a suggested fix, ranked by severity.
misuse: An automated scan reporting zero issues is not a passed audit. Most criteria cannot be checked by a tool.
